subject: chemistry
title: Electrode potentials and electrochemical cells
key_idea: A half-cell has an electrode potential, measured against the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions. Two half-cells joined by a salt bridge make a cell. The cell potential is the more positive electrode potential minus the more negative one.

blocks.text: A half-cell holds a species and its oxidised or reduced form. This section covers what Eᶿ means and the standard hydrogen electrode.

items.meaning: The potential of a half-cell, measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, under standard conditions.
Temperature 298 K, gas pressure 100 kPa and 1.00 mol/dm³ for every ion in solution.
The potential difference (emf) of a cell made from two half-cells under standard conditions.

items: Half-equations for electrodes are written as reductions: oxidised form + ne⁻ ⇌ reduced form. This is the IUPAC convention.
Example: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), Eᶿ = +0.34 V.
The more positive Eᶿ is, the more easily the species on the left is reduced.
The more negative Eᶿ is, the more easily the species on the right is oxidised.

blocks.text: The potential of one half-cell cannot be measured alone. A reference electrode is needed, so every value is measured against the same one.

items: A platinum electrode, coated in platinum black, is dipped in 1.00 mol/dm³ H⁺(aq), usually hydrochloric acid.
Hydrogen gas at 100 kPa is bubbled over the electrode at 298 K.
2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g). Its Eᶿ is defined as 0.00 V.
Platinum is inert and gives a surface where H⁺ and H₂ can exchange electrons.
Eᶿ is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions.
Standard conditions are 298 K, 100 kPa and 1.00 mol/dm³.
Half-equations are written as reductions, with electrons on the left.

blocks.text: Different half-cells need different set-ups. This section covers the three main types and the parts of a cell.

items: A **metal in its ions**: the metal is the electrode and dips in 1.00 mol/dm³ of its ions, for example Zn in Zn²⁺(aq).
A **non-metal and its ions**: gas is bubbled over a platinum electrode in a solution of its ions, for example Cl₂ over Pt in Cl⁻(aq).

**Ions of the same element** in different oxidation states, for example Fe³⁺ and Fe²⁺: both ions are in the same beaker, with a platinum electrode. Their concentrations are equal, usually 1.00 mol/dm³.
The two half-cells are joined by a salt bridge, for example filter paper soaked in potassium nitrate solution. It completes the circuit with moving ions.
A high-resistance voltmeter connects the electrodes, so almost no current flows and the reading is the emf.

blocks.text: The conditions matter. If the temperature, pressure or concentrations change, the electrode potential, E, changes with them.

items: Metals use their own ions. Non-metals and ions of one element use a platinum electrode.
The salt bridge completes the circuit. A high-resistance voltmeter reads the emf.
A change in conditions changes E, so use standard conditions to measure Eᶿ.

blocks.text: Two half-cells make a cell. This section covers how to find the emf and write the diagram.

blocks.label: Standard cell potential
where: The positive electrode has the more positive Eᶿ.
The negative electrode has the more negative Eᶿ.
Eᶿcell is in volts. Do not multiply Eᶿ by the number of electrons.

items: Oxidation happens at the negative electrode. Reduction happens at the positive electrode.
Electrons flow through the external wire from the negative electrode to the positive electrode.
Example: Eᶿcell for Zn and Cu = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
A single line | shows a phase boundary, for example between a solid and a solution.
A double line ‖ shows the salt bridge.
The negative electrode (oxidation) goes on the left. The positive electrode (reduction) goes on the right.
Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) ‖ Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s)
With a platinum electrode: Pt(s) | Fe²⁺(aq), Fe³⁺(aq) ‖ Ag⁺(aq) | Ag(s).
With hydrogen: Pt(s) | H₂(g) | H⁺(aq) ‖ Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s).

diagram.alt: Choose a right-hand and a left-hand half-cell and see the cell potential.

blocks.text: List the half-equations in order of Eᶿ, from the most negative to the most positive. This is the electrochemical series.

items: The reduced forms (right-hand side) at the top, such as Li and Zn, are strong reducing agents.
The oxidised forms (left-hand side) at the bottom, such as F₂ and MnO₄⁻, are strong oxidising agents.
Eᶿcell = Eᶿ(positive) − Eᶿ(negative).
The negative electrode is on the left of a cell diagram. Electrons flow from it.
The electrochemical series ranks half-equations by Eᶿ.

checks.q: State the conditions that define a standard electrode potential.
checks.a: 298 K, 100 kPa pressure for any gas, and 1.00 mol/dm³ concentration of ions.

checks.q: Calculate Eᶿcell for a cell made from Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ (+0.77 V) and Zn²⁺/Zn (−0.76 V), and write its cell diagram.
checks.a: Eᶿcell = +0.77 − (−0.76) = +1.53 V. Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) ‖ Fe³⁺(aq), Fe²⁺(aq) | Pt(s)

checks.q: Explain why a platinum electrode is used in the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ half-cell.
checks.a: Both ions are in solution, so there is no metal electrode. Platinum is inert and conducts, so electrons can pass to or from the ions.

blocks.text: You measure the emf of a cell in the required practical. The Nernst equation is not required.

items.text: Clean each metal. Place each in 1.00 mol/dm³ of its ions.
Connect with a salt bridge and a voltmeter.
Record the voltage. Repeat with other metals and a reference electrode where needed.

blocks.text: Use Eᶿ values to predict the direction of simple redox reactions, calculate cell emf and write the conventional cell representation.
